title: Evidence of positive phototaxis in an adult shrimp offers an opportunity for passive fisheries
content:
Abstract
In many active-gear fisheries, there is an increasing demand for alternative passive gears that reduce bycatch and environmental impact. However, achieving a competitive catch efficiency often remains a major challenge in the development of these gears. In this context, pots combined with artificial light have shown potential in increasing catch rates of several species of decapods. However, the mechanisms involved remain poorly understood. In particular, it is unclear whether light-induced attraction in shrimp results from positive phototaxis or indirect attraction. With the aim of achieving a better understanding of this mechanism, the potential of artificial light to attract brown shrimp (Crangon crangon) was evaluated under laboratory conditions. In the experiments, adult shrimp were released in a starting central compartment from which they could move through funnels to adjacent compartments equipped with either a no-light control, or a white, green, or blue LED light. All tested light colours significantly increased shrimp entry compared to the no-light control, with green moderately outperforming white. In sum, approximately 75% of the individuals left the central compartment towards a light source. An additional experiment changing the position of the lights confirmed that shrimp movement towards the lateral compartments only happened as a response to a light stimulus on the other side of the funnel, providing evidence of positive phototaxis. These findings contribute to the development of light-enhanced passive shrimp fisheries.
